name: France (Fifth Republic)
summary: France under the Fifth Republic, founded by Charles de Gaulle in 1958. After decolonisation it became a founding power of European integration.

location.value: Western Europe, from the Rhine to the Atlantic, plus overseas regions and territories.

terrain.value: Plains, the Alps, Pyrenees and Massif Central.

climate.value: Temperate in the north and west, continental in the east, Mediterranean in the south.

resources.value: Extensive farmland (Europe’s leading agricultural producer) and nuclear power, which generates about 70% of electricity.

disasters.value: The 2003 heatwave killed about 15,000 people; floods and storms.

population.value: Over 69 million (2026), including the overseas regions.

urbanisation.value: Highly urbanised; Paris has a metropolitan population of over 13 million.

disease.value: Universal health care, largely funded by national health insurance; rated among the best in the world by the WHO.

migration.value: Waves of immigration since the early 20th century; from the 1960s–70s many came from North and West Africa.

economicBase.value: A highly diversified economy: services, industry, agriculture and tourism (the world’s top tourist destination).

tradeRoutes.value: Part of the eurozone and the European single market.

wealth.value: A high-income economy; one of the largest in the world.

moneyAndTax.value: Helped establish the eurozone in 1999; uses the euro.

inequality.value: A strong welfare state keeps inequality lower than in many rich countries; tensions in poorer suburbs.

governmentType.value: A semi-presidential republic (the Fifth Republic, founded in 1958).

keyRulers.value: Charles de Gaulle, who founded the Fifth Republic in 1958.

succession.value: The president is directly elected; members of the National Assembly are directly elected for local constituencies.

institutions.value: The Fifth Republic’s 1958 constitution, which strengthened the executive over the legislature.

stability.value: The May 1968 revolt had an enormous social impact.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between left- and right-wing parties, and since 2017 new centrist and populist parties.

armyAndTech.value: A nuclear power with a permanent UN Security Council seat.

majorWars.value: The Algerian War ended in 1962 with Algerian independence.

territoryChange.value: Algeria and most French colonies became independent in the 1960s.

alliancesRivals.value: A leading force in the EU; a founding NATO member that left its joint military command under de Gaulle and later rejoined.

inventions.value: The TGV high-speed train, Concorde (with Britain), Ariane rockets, the Minitel.

scienceEducation.value: Free, secular and compulsory schooling; public universities and selective grandes écoles.

openness.value: Leading role in European integration; open to world culture while protecting French language and film.

communicationTransport.value: The TGV high-speed train, an extensive rail and road network, and the Channel Tunnel to Britain.

religion.value: A secular country (laïcité, since 1905); Catholicism has been the main religion for over a millennium.

languageWriting.value: French, overseen by the Académie Française; regional languages such as Occitan and Breton.

artsArchitecture.value: New Wave cinema (late 1950s–60s), Paris fashion houses, the Centre Pompidou and the Louvre Pyramid.

socialStructure.value: A large middle class; debates about immigration and integration.

sharedIdentity.value: Republican values of “Liberty, Equality, Fraternity” and a strong national culture.

dailyLife.value: Famous wines and cheeses; meals often have three courses.

neighbours.value: Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, Switzerland, Italy, Monaco, Andorra and Spain; a sea border with the UK.

ideasReligions.value: Laïcité (strict separation of church and state, 1905) and existentialist philosophy (Sartre, Camus, de Beauvoir).

colonisation.value: Most colonies became independent in the 1960s; overseas regions and territories remain.

riseSignals.value: De Gaulle’s Fifth Republic (1958) strengthened the executive to end the instability of earlier republics.

peakPeriod.value: The “Trente Glorieuses”, three decades of rapid post-war economic growth.

declineSignals.value: Since the post-Gaullist era, crises with high unemployment and rising public debt.

outcome.value: Continues today as the French Republic.
